newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans embrace opposition parties in state vote.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans embrace opposition parties in state vote.

text.p: Voters in the central state of Morelos appeared to give opposition parties victories in several key cities Sunday in a test of the strength of President Ernesto Zedillo's party.
Early results gave a slight lead to the right-wing National Action Party (PAN) in the race for mayor in the state capital, Cuernevaca, over the governing Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

The PAN obtained 34 percent of the vote in the capital, compared with 31 percent for the PRI and 20 percent for the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) in early results, the state electoral institute said.
The PAN was quick to claim victory in the state capital.
"This is very gratifying to see as it confirms the rebound of the PAN ... (in Cuernavaca)," the president of the PAN, Felipe Calderon Hinojosa, said in a television interview.
The vote in the state was seen as an early referendum on the PRI ahead of wider elections in various states in July.
Despite fears of violence in the mainly rural state just south of Mexico's capital city, the elections in Morelos took place without any reported major incidents.
Voters were being asked to elect 33 mayors and 30 deputies for the local Congress. Before the vote, the PRI held 32 cities and the PRD only one.
Late Sunday, the opposition PRD claimed victory in several large cities in the state, including in Cuautla, the second most important city in the state.
"With no fear of making a mistake, the triumph has been without question for the PRD candidate in Cuautla," PRD president Manuel Lopez Obrador told reporters.
With 860,000 registered voters, Morelos is one of Mexico's smaller states but its proximity to Mexico City gives it a high political profile.
Late Thursday, unknown assailants threw paint thinner in the face and broke the nose of the ruling PRI's mayoral candidate for the city of Cuernavaca.
Voters gave Zedillo's PRI a tough time in the polls in 1995 and 1996, punishing it for the country's dire economic crisis and numerous corruption scandals.
The PRI state governor, Jorge Carrillo Olea, has recently been in the headlines after the New York Times reported he had links to drugs traffickers. He denied the charges.
Carrillo's government has also suffered from citizen protests against a wave of kidnappings in the state.

Once home to peasant leader Emiliano Zapata, who led a revolt during the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, Morelos is now better known as the state that media reports said contained two homes of wanted drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
